slides.headline: Thrown to the lions. Why don't they attack?
slides.sub: Briton Rivière, Daniel in the Lions' Den, 1872

slides.headline: Babylon
slides.text: Babylon. Daniel, a trusted official of King Darius, is caught praying to his God against a royal order. The punishment: the lions.

slides.headline: Daniel
slides.text: His hands are tied. He has no weapon and nowhere to run. He does not fight or beg. He simply stands and waits.

slides.headline: Head bowed
slides.text: His head is bowed. Is it fear, or prayer? Rivière never shows us his eyes, only his stillness.

slides.headline: The lions
slides.text: The lions gather around him, huge and close enough to touch. But look at them: restless, curious, not attacking.

slides.headline: Real beasts
slides.text: Rivière was a famous animal painter. Look at the fur, the muscles, the eyes: these lions feel completely real.

slides.headline: The trap
slides.text: Jealous rivals had pushed the king into that order just to catch Daniel. Darius liked him, but could not take back his own law.

slides.headline: The night
slides.text: In the Bible, the king seals the den with a stone, then spends the whole night unable to eat or sleep.

slides.headline: Morning
slides.text: At dawn, the king runs to the den. Daniel is alive: an angel shut the lions' mouths. Faith, or something else?
